title: Feelings & opinions
goal: Say how you feel, give your opinion, agree and disagree politely, and link ideas with 'because', 'but' and 'so'.
intro:
Pashtuns love a good discussion — about politics, cricket, poetry or the price of flour — and opinions are given frankly but with courtesy. The heart (زړه) is everywhere in Pashto emotional language: زړه مې تنګ دی 'my heart is narrow' means 'I'm bored / fed up', and زړه مې غواړي 'my heart wants' means 'I feel like it'.

In this unit you'll learn emotion words, ways to say 'I think', 'you're right' and 'I don't agree', and the conjunctions that join sentences.

vocab.note: Invariable. مه خفه کېږه 'don't be upset'.
f. په غوسه 'angry'; غوسه کېدل 'to get angry'.
Present: وېرېږم weréẓəm. له … نه وېرېږم 'I'm afraid of …'.
زړه مې تنګ دی 'I'm bored / fed up'.
m. خوند يې راکړ 'I enjoyed it (it gave me taste)'.
m. ستا څه نظر دی؟ 'what do you think?'
f. سمه. ته سم وايې 'you're right'.
In questions also که ka: چای که اوبه؟ 'tea or water?'

phrases.native: زما په فکر دا سمه ده.
phrases.roman: zmā pə fikr dā sáma da.
phrases.en: In my opinion this is right.
Are you serious? (lit. are you telling the truth?)

phrases.native: مه وېرېږه، هر څه به سم شي.
phrases.roman: ma weréẓa, har tsə ba sam shi.
phrases.en: Don't be afraid, everything will be all right.

grammar.title: Giving opinions: 'I think that …'
grammar.body:
The most natural ways to give an opinion are:

**زما په فکر …** zmā pə fikr — 'in my opinion …' (lit. in my thought)
**زه فکر کوم چې …** zə fikr kawə́m che — 'I think that …'
**زما نظر دا دی چې …** — 'my view is that …'

The word **چې** (che) 'that' introduces the clause, exactly like English 'that', and the clause keeps normal word order with its own verb at the end.

To ask someone's opinion: **ستا څه نظر دی؟** / **تاسو څه فکر کوئ؟**. To agree: **سمه ده** 'OK', **ته سم وايې** 'you're right', **زه هم داسې فکر کوم** 'I think so too'. To disagree politely: **زه داسې فکر نه کوم** 'I don't think so', **بښنه غواړم، خو …** 'sorry, but …'.

examples.native: زما په فکر پښتو اسانه ده.
examples.roman: zmā pə fikr paṣtó āsā́na da.

examples.native: زه فکر کوم چې هغه رښتيا وايي.
examples.roman: zə fikr kawə́m che haġá rəṣtyā́ wā́yi.
examples.en: I think he's telling the truth.

examples.native: بښنه غواړم، خو زه داسې فکر نه کوم.
examples.roman: baṣə́na ġwā́ṛəm, xo zə dā́se fikr na kawə́m.
examples.en: Sorry, but I don't think so.

grammar.title: Joining sentences: او، خو، ځکه چې، نو، يا
grammar.body:
**او** aw 'and' · **خو** xo 'but' · **يا** yā 'or' · **نو** no 'so, then' · **ځکه چې** dzə́ka che 'because' · **چې** che 'that; when; so that'.

**ځکه چې** introduces the reason: زه خوشاله يم ځکه چې ورور مې راغلی 'I'm happy because my brother has come'. On its own, **ځکه** means 'that's why': ورور مې راغلی، ځکه خوشاله يم.

The question 'why?' is **ولې** (wə́le); the answer starts with ځکه چې.

**خو** is very frequent and also works as a softening, emphatic particle in second position: زه خو نه ځم 'well, *I'm* not going'.

examples.native: ولې خفه يې؟ ځکه چې زما ملګری لاړ.
examples.roman: wə́le xapá ye? dzə́ka che zmā malgə́ray lāṛ.
examples.en: Why are you sad? Because my friend has left.

examples.native: باران ورېږي، نو کور کې پاتې کېږو.
examples.roman: bārā́n wréẓi, no kor ke pā́te kéẓu.
examples.en: It's raining, so we'll stay at home.

examples.native: زه نه وېرېږم ځکه چې ته له ما سره يې.
examples.roman: zə na weréẓəm dzə́ka che tə la mā sara ye.
examples.en: I'm not afraid because you're with me.

dialogue.title: After the cricket match
dialogue.setting: Naqib and Jawad have just watched Afghanistan play on TV.

lines.speaker: Naqib
lines.native: ډېر خوند يې راکړ! زه ډېر خوشاله يم.
lines.roman: ḍer xwand ye rā́kaṛ! zə ḍer xoshā́la yəm.
lines.en: That was great! I'm so happy.

lines.speaker: Jawad
lines.native: هو، خو زما په فکر لومړۍ برخه ښه نه وه. ډېر ناوخته يې منډې جوړې کړې.
lines.roman: ho, xo zmā pə fikr lumṛə́y bərxa ṣa na wa. ḍer nāwáxta ye mánḍe jóṛe kṛe.
lines.en: Yes, but I think the first innings wasn't good. They made their runs too late.

lines.speaker: Naqib
lines.native: ته سم وايې، خو په پای کې ډېر ښه ولوبېدل.
lines.roman: tə sam wā́ye, xo pə pāy ke ḍer ṣə wə́lobedəl.
lines.en: You're right, but at the end they played really well.

lines.speaker: Jawad
lines.native: رښتيا. ستا څه نظر دی، بل ميچ به هم وګټو؟
lines.roman: rəṣtyā́. stā tsə nazár day, bəl mich ba ham wə́gaṭu?
lines.en: True. What do you think — will we win the next match too?

lines.speaker: Naqib
lines.native: زه فکر کوم چې هو، ځکه چې زموږ لوبغاړي ځوان او قوي دي.
lines.roman: zə fikr kawə́m che ho, dzə́ka che zmuẓ lobġā́ṛi dzwān aw qawí di.
lines.en: I think so, because our players are young and strong.

lines.speaker: Jawad
lines.native: انشاالله! نو بل ځل به سره ګورو.
lines.roman: inshāllā́h! no bəl dzal ba sara góru.
lines.en: God willing! So we'll watch the next one together.

culture: Cricket has become a passion across the Pashtun world: many of Afghanistan's national team are Pashtuns who learned the game in refugee camps in Pakistan, and the team's rise is a source of huge national pride. In conversation, open disagreement with an elder is avoided — younger people say 'you're right, but …' or stay silent — while among friends lively argument is normal and enjoyed. Strong emotions are often expressed through poetry: a well-chosen *landay* (folk couplet) or a line of Rahman Baba can say what plain words cannot. Men and women express feelings with more restraint in public than in private.
